## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.78205.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.78205.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Monkeys exhibit human-like gaze biases in economic decisions" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Michael Frank as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

Below are three specific points, distilled from the attached reviews, considered essential revisions for the authors to address. The individual reviews appended below can be consulted for further elaboration on these points and additional suggestions to improve the manuscript.

1. A general concern is that the value associated with an item can potentially attract gaze independent of choice, and reviewers felt that these relationships should be considered in more detail (addressed primarily by R1 and R3). On one hand, given a limited set of values, value difference is highly correlated with both the options and the chosen value, and it is suggested that the authors attempt to disentangle these in their results. Similarly, effects on fixation duration should be explored in more detail, including whether they relate to only one of the option values or both, and how they vary when there are 2 versus 3 fixations in a choice. Finally, it was felt that there should be additional discussion of the complex interplay in which a valuable item attracts attention and attention to an item may also increase its subjective value, and the extent to which these possibilities are disentangled or confounded in the current data. (Note that this final concern may be somewhat addressed by the analyses suggested in point 3 below).

2. A second concern is that the approach to "non-decision time" was viewed as arbitrary and perhaps not entirely valid (addressed primarily by R2 and R1). The current approach assumes that final and non-final fixations should be the same length, although other work has shown that final fixations are generally shorter. It also assumes that motor preparation time is equal across all chosen values, although higher values typically motivate faster motor responses. Point 3 below makes a suggestion about how to consider NDT in alternative choice models. Other potential approaches to address this concern within the present model include testing different estimates for NDTs and demonstrating the robustness of the overall results.

3. Finally, reviewers felt that the study would be strengthened by additional exploration of their data in light of studies that assess whether gaze might directly increase drift rate (i.e., gaze is additive to value), rather than (or in addition to) multiplicative effects, where gaze amplifies the attended value. (See Cavanagh et al. 2014 JEP General, Gluth et al. 2018 eLife, and Smith and Krajbich 2019 Psych Sci.)

Specifically, Westbrook et al. (Science, 2020) suggested a hybrid two stage model whereby gaze is multiplicative on value early during choice and additive later, with a rationale similar to that discussed here ("post-decisional gaze anchoring" – see also recent work by Callaway et al. 2021 PLoS CB for a related but more continuous model). The central assumption of GLAM is that gaze weights the impact of value on evidence accumulation, but given the issues regarding NDT, considering other models in one way or another is important, and the authors have the trial counts to do so quantitatively. Thus, the authors should address the issue of whether gaze effects in monkeys are multiplicative as assumed by GLAM, or whether they might be additive when applied to the data. There was extensive discussion on this topic in consultation, and indeed there is evidence for both in the human literature. Clearly, publication decisions will not depend on the conclusions of this exploration per se, but a strength of the current data set is that it may be able to speak to this unresolved issue.

One consideration in undertaking such an alternative model analysis is that it could be done with and without truncating NDT (so that NDT would be captured by the second phase of a 2-phase model) and/or by better justifying the choice of NDT. Moreover, it was felt that a model/parameter recovery analysis is a critical component of these explorations. In other words, if Model A "wins", simulated data from model A should be able to reproduce key features of the data that Model B cannot capture, and vice versa and parameter estimates should be recoverable when fitting to those data (see Wilson and Collins 2019 eLife).

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Critique 1: The authors should consider the possibility that unique option values can explain putative effects of value difference. One approach might be to subselect trials and analyze data sets where chosen value varies but value difference is constant and vice versa.

Critique 2: The concern about whether effect first fixated values carry over into behavior during the second fixation could be addressed similarly to critique 1 or with model comparison approaches.

Critique 3: The authors should consider whether a more flexible definition of NDTs could better fit behavior. This concern might also be addressed in approaches to critique 4.

Critique 4: The concern in this critique is that value and choice can have influence on gaze behavior (and drift rates) that is not accounted for by the present models. Addressing this would involve more extensive re-analysis than the previous points, however given that the contribution of this paper is showing that monkey behavior recapitulates what has been reported in humans, I think it is warranted to explore more complex interactions between gaze and choice that have been found in humans subjects. To address this concern, the authors should consider comparing the present results to models that allow the γ parameter to vary with specific task parameters (for instance as in Westbrook, 2020).

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

It seems a little silly to expend all this effort generating bootstrapped distributions of final and non-final fixation differences, only to then arbitrarily choose the 95th percentile of that distribution as the terminal non decision time. Why not instead either simply get the best estimate you can from the literature, and/or demonstrate the robustness of the results to different non-decision time corrections (e.g. 0, 200, 400 ms)?

Regarding the manipulation where onsets were staggered: the analysis here seemed convoluted. Why not directly test whether subjects were more likely to choose the initially presented option? Figure 3 helps to address this, but leaves some ambiguity for Monkey K, who doesn't always initially fixate on the first presented alternative.

It may be worth noting that the effects in Figure 5 appear to be smaller than in most human data. This might be an argument for 'not' cutting the last 200ms of each trial?

On page 28 the authors discuss Krajbich et al. 2021 and argue that their findings are consistent with LIP, frontal eye fields, and the superior colliculus accumulating evidence in studies where eyes are used to report decisions. However, that study was like this one; subjects were free to look around but they chose using the keyboard.

I thought the authors missed an opportunity to discuss some of the human neuroimaging work on value-based SSM, given the focus of their Discussion section. There are a number of well-known articles that are relevant, for example:

Hare et al. 2011 (PNAS); Gluth et al. 2012 (J Neuro); Rodriguez et al. 2015 (European J Neurosci); Pisauro et al. 2017 (Nature Comm).

Why did the authors use different delays for the two monkeys?

How long were the delays between releasing the center lever and pressing left or right?

Was there some criterion for passing the training stage?

p.33-34 – these numbers should go in the Results section, not the Methods.

I think it might make sense to include session-level random effects in the models, given that each session used a different set of stimuli. I doubt this will change much, but it might further help clean up some variance.

p.38 – This argument about how early gaze might be used to explore and evaluate targets while late gaze is used to focus on the to-be-chosen target comes nearly straight out of Westbrook et al. 2020 (Science).

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

I would have liked to see a more extensive discussion of what might underly the observed effects. The sequential sampling models are merely descriptive. One would like to know how fixation influences the neural signals that compute the value of the option. When a human/monkey is looking at one option, information about a previously viewed option must be maintained in working memory and the neural signals might be expected to be noisier, leading to a bias towards the most recently viewed option. Similarly, the first viewed option might have a stronger signal than the second viewed item by virtue of having less interference. This is obviously speculative but it would be nice to see what evidence there is for something like this – indeed the McGinty et al. 2016 paper seems to provide evidence of this kind. One could argue that it shouldn't be too surprising that computations performed at the fixation point are higher S/N than ones off fixation. (In the context of the sequential sampling model this would correspond to adding some noise to the item not currently fixated.)

Related to this, the discussion of how the paradigm might be used for further exploration is a bit vague. The example given of MT and LIP is not particularly well chosen, given the recent evidence from the Huk lab (Katz et al., Nature 2016) against LIP as the site of the perceptual decision.

Another general concern is the absence of any discussion of all the work showing that value associated with an item serves to attract gaze and indeed is a central aspect of the mechanisms of gaze control and learning where to attend. One closely related example is the work of Hikosaka (eg Kim et al., Cell, 2015) showing that cells in the caudate tail coded the value of previously rewarded fractal patterns and attracted gaze. This makes the question of causality a bit difficult to disentangle. It's such a central issue that it needs to be explicitly discussed. Having the stimuli not resolvable in the peripheral retina helps with this issue.

I would also like to see more of the actual fixation time data. If there are only two fixations, having a bias towards the first one viewed is in conflict with a bias towards the last one viewed. Thus it would be nice to see the fixation durations broken down into cases where there are 2 fixations and cases where there are 3 fixations. Just as the calculation that the initial-view bias is equal to about half a drop of juice, it would also be useful to know how fixation duration translates to choice bias. If I am understanding Figure 4 correctly it looks like an extra 200 msec viewing time translates to about a 10% increase in choice probability. More concrete description of the fixations would be helpful. For example, how do the β values on p8-9 translate to fixation durations?

claims.claim: Sequential sampling models are a highly successful class of models used to explain simple decision behaviors.
claims.source: While the neural mechanisms linking gaze and economic choice are not fully known, the underlying computations have been explored using sequential sampling models, a highly successful class of models used to explain simple decision behaviors (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about sequential sampling models, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In sequential sampling models, a stream of noisy evidence for each option is accumulated until one item accrues enough evidence to reach a pre-defined threshold.
claims.source: In these models, a stream of noisy evidence for each option is accumulated until one item accrues enough evidence to reach a pre-defined threshold, and a decision is rendered in favor of that item.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how sequential sampling models work, representing established knowledge.

claims.claim: For value-based tasks, the evidence accumulation rate can be formulated as a function of the relative value of the possible outcomes.
claims.source: For value-based tasks, the evidence accumulation rate can be formulated as a function of the relative value of the possible outcomes—the larger the difference in relative value, the faster that evidence accumulates for the higher valued item.
claims.evidence: This describes how sequential sampling models are applied to value-based tasks.

claims.claim: The larger the difference in relative value, the faster that evidence accumulates for the higher valued item.

claims.claim: Attentional sequential sampling models (aSSMs) assume that evidence for a given item accumulates at a faster rate while that item is being viewed.
claims.source: These models, collectively referred to as attentional sequential sampling models (aSSMs), assume that evidence for a given item accumulates at a faster rate while that item is being viewed, and accumulates slower when it is not being viewed (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Smith and Krajbich, 2018; Tavares et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the key assumption of aSSMs, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In aSSMs, evidence accumulates slower when an item is not being viewed.
claims.source: These models, collectively referred to as attentional sequential sampling models (aSSMs), assume that evidence for a given item accumulates at a faster rate while that item is being viewed, and accumulates slower when it is not being viewed (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Smith and Krajbich, 2018; Tavares et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the key assumption of aSSMs, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: aSSMs have been successful in accounting for human gaze biases across several decision-making domains.
claims.source: Overall, these models have been successful in accounting for human gaze biases across several decision-making domains (Krajbich, 2019; Manohar and Husain, 2013; Smith and Krajbich, 2018; Thomas et al., 2019; Westbrook et al., 2020), supporting the idea that gaze modulates the decision process by biasing an evidence accumulation process.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior modeling studies.

claims.claim: Intracranial recordings in nonhuman primates are an ideal approach for identifying candidate neural substrates of gaze biases.
claims.source: To identify candidate neural substrates, intracranial recordings in nonhuman primates (NHPs) are an ideal approach, as they combine an animal model with human-like oculomotor behavior with the high temporal resolution necessary to accommodate the rapid pace of natural eye movements (Kravitz et al., 2013; Ongür and Price, 2000; Wise, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a reasoned argument supported by citations about NHP neurophysiology.

claims.claim: Humans show three core choice biases related to gaze behavior: initial fixation bias, cumulative gaze-time bias, and final fixation bias.
claims.source: Humans show three core choice biases related to gaze behavior. First, they tend to choose the item that they viewed first (initial fixation bias). Second, they tend to choose the item they spend more time looking at over the course of the trial (cumulative gaze-time bias). Third, they tend to choose in favor of the target they are viewing at the moment they indicate their choice.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from prior human studies.

results.result: A novel value-based choice task was developed for macaque monkeys in which they freely view targets using eye movements and indicate choices via manual lever press. The task includes gaze-contingent masking and visual crowders to ensure targets must be directly fixated for value information to be available.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C37-C43, C148-C149 collectively describe the experimental design with sufficient detail. The task design is well-documented with clear procedural steps, sample sizes (54 sessions, ~30,000 trials), and methodological rationale. The gaze-contingent masking and crowder features are novel elements that distinguish this paradigm from prior NHP studies.

results.result: Monkeys showed value-dependent choice behavior with near-optimal performance on easy trials (>98% correct for value differences of ±3-4 drops) and 86% correct on difficult trials (±1-2 drops). Choice behavior was well-described by a logistic function of value difference (β=1.37, p<1e-10).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 provide converging evidence of behavioral control with appropriate statistical support. The logistic regression analysis (C48) with highly significant p-values and the graded performance across difficulty levels (C44-C45) demonstrate that monkeys understood the task contingencies. The low lapse rate inference (C47) is appropriately supported by near-chance performance on equal-value trials (C46).

results.result: Reaction time and number of fixations were modulated by task difficulty, with slower responses and more fixations for difficult trials. When difficulty and chosen value were independently assessed, RT was more strongly modulated by chosen value (CPD=8%) than difficulty (CPD=1.4%), while fixation number showed the opposite pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C58 describe a sophisticated analysis that appropriately addresses the confound between difficulty and chosen value (C53). The residualization approach (described in C54-C56) is methodologically sound, and the statistical results are well-supported with confidence intervals and p-values. The dissociation between RT and fixation number (C57-C58) is a meaningful finding, though the interpretation remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: Monkeys almost always viewed both targets (>91% of trials) and made an average of 2.45-2.57 fixations per trial, which is fewer than the ~3.7 fixations typically observed in human binary choice tasks. The majority of trials contained either 2 or 3 total fixations.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 provide clear descriptive statistics about fixation patterns. The comparison to human data (C65) is appropriately qualified as coming from prior studies. The data are internally consistent and the percentages sum appropriately (C60-C61). This establishes an important species difference that is discussed later in the manuscript.

results.result: Fixation durations decreased with absolute order in the trial (β=-0.049, p<1.92e-9) and were longer for final versus non-final fixations (β=-0.047, p<1e-10) after controlling for the other factor. The prolonged final fixations in monkeys differ from humans but may be explained by monkeys making fewer total fixations.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 describe a careful analysis that appropriately separates absolute and relative order effects using residualization. The statistical support is strong. Claims C70-C71 acknowledge an apparent discrepancy with human data and provide a reasonable mechanistic explanation based on the difference in total fixation numbers. The explanation is logical but remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Fixation durations were modulated by target values in a position-dependent manner. First fixations increased with fixated value (β=0.003, p=0.0007), while middle fixations decreased with fixated value (β=-0.0076, p<1e-10) and were influenced by non-fixated value (β=-0.035, p<1e-10). Middle fixations increased with relative value (β=0.016, p<1e-10) and decreased with difficulty (β=-0.019, p<1e-10).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 provide detailed statistical evidence for value effects on fixation durations with appropriate p-values and confidence intervals. The pattern is complex but internally consistent. Claims C78-C79 draw appropriate inferences about the interdependence of fixation and valuation processes, which is important for interpreting gaze biases. The statistical support is robust across multiple analyses.

results.result: Evidence supports a two-stage model of gaze bias: final fixations were prolonged and directed to the chosen target (~97% of trials). Model comparison showed multiplicative and additive models fit similarly without truncation, but multiplicative fit better with ≥100ms truncation (100% probability at 100ms), supporting a transition from multiplicative to additive gaze bias ~100ms before response.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 describe a systematic model comparison approach with clear results. The behavioral observations (C91-C92) are well-documented. The modeling analysis (C93-C97) uses appropriate methods (GLAM framework, WAIC comparison) and shows a clear pattern across truncation values. The 100ms NDT estimate (C98) is derived from data and is consistent with prior literature on gaze-anchoring. The logic is sound and well-supported.

results.result: Monkeys showed an initial fixation bias: they were more likely to choose the first-viewed item (β=0.66, p=0.00015), equivalent to 0.47 drops of juice. Initial fixations were unbiased with respect to value. A gaze manipulation experiment using staggered target onsets successfully induced initial fixation bias (β=0.70, p=3.02e-06) with comparable magnitude to spontaneous bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 establish the initial fixation bias with appropriate statistics and demonstrate that it cannot be attributed to value-driven fixation patterns (C102-C103). The gaze manipulation experiment (C105-C110) provides causal evidence with proper controls (no main effect of trial type, C107-C108) and comparable effect sizes. This is strong converging evidence for a causal role of initial fixation. The experimental design and analysis are rigorous.

results.result: Monkeys showed a cumulative gaze-time bias: they were more likely to choose items viewed longer (β=18.71, p<1e-10). After correcting for value effects on viewing time, the relationship remained significant (β=1.07, p<1e-10) and was robust to NDT truncation up to 200ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 demonstrate the cumulative gaze-time bias with strong statistical support. The value-correction procedure (C112) appropriately addresses the confound between value and viewing time identified earlier (C78-C79). The robustness analysis (C114) strengthens confidence in the finding. The effect size interpretation (~5% change in choice probability for 0.2s viewing time difference) is reasonable.

results.result: Using NDT-truncated data, monkeys showed a final fixation bias: they were more likely to choose the target being viewed at the virtual trial end (β=3.35, p<1e-10). This effect persisted with up to 200ms truncation, suggesting it can be partially explained by gaze effects on evidence accumulation rather than solely post-decision gaze attraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 demonstrate the final fixation bias with appropriate statistical support and careful consideration of the NDT issue. The robustness to 200ms truncation (C118) is important for distinguishing pre-decision from post-decision gaze effects. The interpretation (C119) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging that the effect can be "at least in part" explained by evidence accumulation. The analysis is methodologically sound.

results.result: An attentional sequential sampling model (GLAM) with gaze bias fit the data significantly better than a model without gaze bias (dWAIC: -3357.9 and -8159.7 for the two monkeys). The gaze bias parameter (γ) distributions in monkeys fully overlapped with human distributions. The model made accurate out-of-sample predictions of choice, RT, and gaze-bias effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C127 provide comprehensive computational modeling evidence. The model comparison (C120-C121) uses appropriate methods (WAIC) with clear results. The cross-species comparison (C122) is illustrated in Figure 8 and shows substantial overlap. The out-of-sample validation (C123-C124, C127) is rigorous and demonstrates that the model captures key behavioral patterns. The control analysis showing that a no-gaze-bias model fails to capture cumulative gaze effects (C124) is important. This is strong evidence for shared mechanisms across species.

results.result: Monkeys exhibited gaze biases qualitatively and quantitatively similar to humans, and these biases were well-explained by the same sequential sampling model framework (aSSM) used in humans. This suggests a common mechanism for gaze-related choice biases across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C12, C131, and C184 represent the primary conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergence of evidence from: (1) three distinct gaze biases matching human patterns, (2) successful modeling with the same framework used in humans, (3) overlapping model parameters across species, and (4) causal manipulation of initial fixation. The evidence is comprehensive and the conclusions are appropriately stated.

results.result: Two differences in gaze behavior between monkeys and humans were identified: monkeys made fewer fixations per trial (~2.5 vs ~3.7) and showed prolonged final fixations (opposite to humans). These differences may be related, as early-trial fixations are longer in both species, and monkeys' final fixations occur earlier in the trial sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C136 acknowledge important species differences and provide a mechanistic explanation. The explanation (C136) is logical and consistent with the data on fixation duration by absolute order (C66-C67). However, this remains somewhat speculative as it is based on cross-study comparisons rather than direct within-study manipulation. The acknowledgment of these differences is important for interpreting the overall similarity claim.

results.result: The data are most consistent with a two-stage aSSM where gaze initially biases choice multiplicatively, then transitions to an additive mode where gaze is drawn to the chosen target. This second stage is consistent with gaze-anchoring, a motor-preparatory phenomenon. The estimated 100ms transition point aligns with gaze-anchoring latencies (64-100ms) from prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 synthesize the modeling results (from C93-C97) with prior literature on gaze-anchoring. The interpretation is well-supported by the model comparison data and is consistent with established findings about motor preparation (C139-C140). The convergence between the data-driven NDT estimate and prior gaze-anchoring latencies (C141) strengthens the interpretation. This provides a mechanistic framework for understanding the gaze biases.

results.result: The true duration of the post-decision epoch is difficult to estimate from behavioral data alone, and additional work will be necessary to confirm the robustness of the measured gaze bias effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the behavioral approach for estimating NDT. This is an honest assessment of uncertainty. However, the robustness analyses showing effects persist up to 200ms truncation (C114, C118) provide some confidence. The call for additional work is appropriate and does not undermine the main findings.

results.result: The study demonstrates that initial fixation has a causal effect on choice through gaze manipulation, and the aSSM modeling provides a mechanistic explanation that permits direct comparison to human studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C147 summarize key contributions of the study. The causal evidence from the gaze manipulation experiment (C105-C110) is strong, and the modeling framework (C120-C127) enables quantitative cross-species comparison. These represent important advances over prior NHP studies that lacked these features.

results.result: The novel task is well-suited for neural mechanistic studies such as electrophysiological recordings or stimulation, and will make it possible to identify cell- and circuit-level mechanisms of gaze biases.
results.evaluation: Claims C132 and C185 represent forward-looking conclusions about the utility of the paradigm. These are well-supported by the demonstration of: (1) behavioral control (C128-C130), (2) human-comparable gaze biases (C9, C131), and (3) successful computational modeling (C125-C127). The task meets the stated criteria for an animal model suitable for mechanistic studies. However, the actual identification of neural mechanisms (C185) remains future work.
